claims.text: Reducing Ta content in TiZrHfTax destabilizes the bcc phase.
A reduced-Ta TiZrHfTax alloy can begin as a metastable single-phase bcc material near a second-phase instability.
Applied mechanical stress initiates a partial bcc-to-hcp phase transformation in the metastable alloy.
The stress-induced transformation forms nanoscale hcp precipitates within the bcc matrix.
Stress-induced bcc-to-hcp transformation is the primary mechanism responsible for improved dynamic mechanical performance.
The transformation increases the dynamic strain-hardening rate relative to a stable single-phase alloy.
The metastable transforming alloy has greater ductility than the stable single-phase baseline under identical loading conditions.
Hcp precipitates in TiZrHfTax have enhanced resistance to shear and thereby promote strengthening.
The hcp precipitates strengthen the alloy specifically by obstructing dislocation motion.
The hcp precipitates accommodate deformation while resisting shear.
Twinning and slip in regions adjacent to the hcp precipitates maintain ductility.
A higher-Ta, compositionally similar alloy remains a single bcc phase during deformation and does not undergo stress-induced transformation.
In situ characterization will detect nucleation and growth of hcp regions under load in the metastable alloy but not in the stable baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies generally to multi-principal-element alloys located near a phase-instability threshold.
The mechanism operates only over strain-rate and temperature ranges that permit stress-induced transformation kinetics.
Very low or very high temperatures, or compositions far from the instability threshold, may suppress the mechanism.
The magnitude of strengthening and ductility enhancement depends on alloy composition, processing history, and test conditions.
Rapid loading may alter or limit the kinetics of the proposed phase transformation.
